Sept 24 (Reuters) - US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to ​the talks said.

The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the ‌global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.

# Iran, US end UN talks still divided as Hormuz blockade continues



Iran and the United States ended Wednesday divided over how to end their war despite renewed UN talks, as Tehran rejected US pressure and Washington maintained its blockade of Iranian ports while oil shipments continued through Hormuz.

The first indirect talks between the two countries in months took place Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, between speeches in which US President Donald Trump threatened further military action and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian rejected the use of force to secure a deal.

Pezeshkian told the assembly Wednesday that Iran would not surrender to American pressure but remained willing to negotiate. He accused Trump of displaying a “bullying mentality” and argued that diplomacy could not succeed under military threats.

His address left the central dispute unresolved. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran was reviewing Washington’s response to its proposal for ending hostilities but that the sides remained far apart. The proposal prioritizes lifting the US blockade of Iranian ports and reopening Hormuz.

Trump had described Tuesday’s discussions as productive. Iranian officials confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi communicated with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner through Qatari mediation but disputed suggestions that Tehran had abandoned its conditions for reopening the strait.

**Hormuz remains at the center of the dispute*

events.content_detail:
# Zelensky says the Trump administration proposes a halt to energy strikes, a Black Sea grain corridor, and three-way talks with Russia

The Trump administration is pressing for three immediate steps to de-escalate the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios.

First, the U.S. has proposed that Moscow and Kyiv agree to a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure.

Washington is also seeking to reopen the Black Sea grain corridor and hold trilateral talks involving the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine.

Axios said Abu Dhabi was a possible venue for the talks. Kyiv is ready to accept Abu Dhabi as a venue. “We are open — any country, any format,” Zelensky said.

Zelensky said the G20 summit in Miami this December could also be a venue for a trilateral meeting. He and Donald Trump discussed that possibility. Zelensky said he still doubts Vladimir Putin is willing to negotiate and believes Putin “could find reasons” to avoid a meeting of the three countries’ leaders.

A source familiar with the matter told Axios that Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on September 24 to meet with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the latest U.S. proposals.

The Ukrainian outlet ZN.UA [said](https://t.me/znua_live/265860), citing diplomatic sources, that a trilateral meeting is being arranged in New York between Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president’s office, and U.S. and Russian special envoys Steve Witkoff and Kirill Dmitriev. Russi

# Hunger on the Horizon: The New Black Sea Grain Crisis

Recent escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war has halted the Black Sea grain trade and metastasized into a war on the global food system. Combined with drought in the Northern Hemisphere, a looming super El Niño, and persistent instability in the Middle East—the world is on the verge of a crisis that could erase years of progress in reducing global hunger and push millions into acute food insecurity.

![People look on as smoke rises from a civilian vessel on fire, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine, on July 28, 2026.](https://assets.cfr.org/images/t_cfr_3_2/f_auto/w_1920/v1790195462/BlackSeaGrainCrisis_01/BlackSeaGrainCrisis_01.jpg)

*Sam Henry Lazarus traveled to Ukraine in March 2026 in support of this article. As a geoeconomic analyst at the Council on Foreign Relations, his research focuses on U.S. national security and the intersection of markets and geopolitics.*

ANKARA, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskiy that attacks by Russia and Ukraine on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were inexplicable and steps must ​be taken to stop these, according to a readout from his office ‌on Thursday.

"During the ​meeting, President Erdogan stated that Turkey was ready to do all it can ​for the Ukraine-Russia war to end with lasting peace, that we will ⁠continue our efforts to revive direct negotiations," the Turkish presidency said in a statement.

# Five questions hanging over Trump’s meeting with Xi

In today’s issue:

▪ Xi’s state visit kicks off

▪ Judge strikes down media ban

▪ Debate over how to tackle diesel costs

▪ Forecasters shift races toward Democrats

Chinese President Xi Jinping is meeting with President Trump today for high-stakes talks that could touch on several points of tension between their countries, including artificial intelligence and weapons shipments to Taiwan.

The state visit is Xi’s first to the U.S. in a decade, coming just four months after Trump’s own visit to China in May. The pair of global leaders appeared to improve relations during that summit, though there were few signs of progress on a trade deal.

The world will be watching closely to see if the pomp and pageantry leads to any breakthroughs this time around.

Here’s five questions surrounding Trump’s meeting with Xi:

Will Trump, Xi agree to AI hotline?

The rising fears around the growth of AI have added to the anticipation around the superpower summit, with members of both parties expressing concern about the technology getting out of control.

Trump’s approach to the concerns has largely been to brush them aside, emphasizing that the U.S. must win an AI arms race with China, which is viewed as the U.S.’s top competitor. One safeguard that the administration seems to be open to is the creation of an AI hotline to establish a point of cooperation between the U.S. and China.
